Emulating targets features

Source: vignettes/articles/v07b-emulate-targets.Rmd
v07b-emulate-targets.Rmd

The comparison with targets lists several features that {targets} has and {pipeflow} does not: file tracking, metadata, runs in a fresh R process, and more. Many of them can be emulated with existing {pipeflow} functions and a few lines of your own code. This article shows one recipe per feature. Each section names the {targets} feature, shows the recipe as running code, and says where the emulation stops.

library(pipeflow)

File targets

In {targets}, a target with format = "file" tracks a file: when the file changes, the target and everything downstream of it run again.

{pipeflow} doesn’t look at files. But it does notice when a parameter changes. So give the step that reads the file an extra parameter, here rev, that it ignores, and set it to a fingerprint of the file before each run.

path <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
write.csv(data.frame(x = 1:3), path, row.names = FALSE)

p <- pip_new("files") |>
    pip_add("read", \(path, rev = NULL) read.csv(path),
        params = list(path = path)
    ) |>
    pip_add("total", \(data = ~read) sum(data$x))

refresh <- function(p) {
    pip_set_params(p, list(rev = unname(tools::md5sum(path))))
}

The first run computes everything.

refresh(p)
p
# <pipeflow> files (2 steps)
# --------------------------
#     step   params depends state
# 1:  read path,rev           new
# 2: total     data    read   new
# --------------------------
# <ready> last run: never
# steps: 2 new
pip_run(p)
# info [2026-10-26 16:31:46.372 UTC]: Starting run of pipeflow 'files'
# info [2026-10-26 16:31:46.372 UTC]: Step 1/2 read
# info [2026-10-26 16:31:46.375 UTC]: Step 2/2 total
# info [2026-10-26 16:31:46.375 UTC]: Finished in 0.003 s (2 done, 0 skipped, 0 failed)

Setting a parameter to the value it already has is not a change (see Setting Identical Values). So if the file is unchanged, refresh() leaves the states alone and nothing runs.

refresh(p)
p
# <pipeflow> files (2 steps)
# --------------------------
#     step   params depends state               out
# 1:  read path,rev          done <data.frame[3x1]>
# 2: total     data    read  done                 6
# --------------------------
# <ready> last run: 2026-10-26 16:31:46 (0.003 s)
# steps: 2 done
pip_run(p)
# info [2026-10-26 16:31:46.459 UTC]: Starting run of pipeflow 'files'
# info [2026-10-26 16:31:46.459 UTC]: Step 1/2 read - skipping done step
# info [2026-10-26 16:31:46.459 UTC]: Step 2/2 total - skipping done step
# info [2026-10-26 16:31:46.459 UTC]: Finished in 0.001 s (0 done, 2 skipped, 0 failed)

Once the file is edited, its fingerprint changes. refresh() outdates the step that reads it and all steps downstream of it.

write.csv(data.frame(x = 1:4), path, row.names = FALSE)

refresh(p)
p
# <pipeflow> files (2 steps)
# --------------------------
#     step   params depends    state               out
# 1:  read path,rev         outdated <data.frame[3x1]>
# 2: total     data    read outdated                 6
# --------------------------
# <ready> last run: 2026-10-26 16:31:46 (0.001 s)
# steps: 2 outdated
pip_run(p)
# info [2026-10-26 16:31:46.532 UTC]: Starting run of pipeflow 'files'
# info [2026-10-26 16:31:46.532 UTC]: Step 1/2 read
# info [2026-10-26 16:31:46.535 UTC]: Step 2/2 total
# info [2026-10-26 16:31:46.537 UTC]: Finished in 0.005 s (2 done, 0 skipped, 0 failed)
p[["total", "out"]]
# [1] 10

To refresh and run in one go, use refresh(p) |> pip_run().

Variants. file.mtime() and file.size() are cheaper than tools::md5sum(), because they don’t read the file. They are also less reliable: a copy or a git checkout changes the modification time without changing the content, and an edit can keep the size. For several files, tools::md5sum(c(path1, path2)) returns one hash per file, and any change in the vector outdates the step. If different steps read different files, give each its own parameter (raw_rev, lookup_rev, …).

Limits.

  • The fingerprint is only as fresh as the last refresh(). Forget to call it, and an edited file goes unnoticed.
  • Only files that steps read are covered. {targets} also notices when a file that a target wrote was changed or deleted. Here you have to rerun that step yourself.

Rebuild when code changes

{targets} reruns a target when its command or a function it calls changes, including your own helper functions.

In {pipeflow}, replacing a step function with pip_replace() already outdates the step and its downstream steps. What {pipeflow} can’t see is a helper function that the step calls. Use the same trick as for files, with a hash of the helper as fingerprint.

clean <- function(x) round(x, 1)

p <- pip_new("code") |>
    pip_add("data", \(n = 4) seq_len(n) / 3) |>
    pip_add("cleaned", \(x = ~data, code = NULL) clean(x))

refresh_code <- function(p) {
    pip_set_params(p, list(code = rlang::hash(utils::removeSource(clean))))
}

refresh_code(p) |> pip_run(lgr = NULL)
p
# <pipeflow> code (2 steps)
# -------------------------
#       step params depends state                                     out
# 1:    data      n          done 0.3333333,0.6666667,1.0000000,1.3333333
# 2: cleaned x,code    data  done                         0.3,0.7,1.0,1.3
# -------------------------
# <ready> last run: 2026-10-26 16:31:46 (0.002 s)
# steps: 2 done

removeSource() matters: in an interactive session, R keeps the source code of every function you define, and the hash would cover it. Then running the same definition again would change the hash. Without the source, defining the same helper again changes nothing:

clean <- function(x) round(x, 1)

refresh_code(p)
p
# <pipeflow> code (2 steps)
# -------------------------
#       step params depends state                                     out
# 1:    data      n          done 0.3333333,0.6666667,1.0000000,1.3333333
# 2: cleaned x,code    data  done                         0.3,0.7,1.0,1.3
# -------------------------
# <ready> last run: 2026-10-26 16:31:46 (0.002 s)
# steps: 2 done

A new version of the helper outdates the step that calls it.

clean <- function(x) round(x, 2)

refresh_code(p)
p
# <pipeflow> code (2 steps)
# -------------------------
#       step params depends    state                                     out
# 1:    data      n             done 0.3333333,0.6666667,1.0000000,1.3333333
# 2: cleaned x,code    data outdated                         0.3,0.7,1.0,1.3
# -------------------------
# <ready> last run: 2026-10-26 16:31:46 (0.002 s)
# steps: 1 done, 1 outdated
pip_run(p)
# info [2026-10-26 16:31:46.757 UTC]: Starting run of pipeflow 'code'
# info [2026-10-26 16:31:46.757 UTC]: Step 1/2 data - skipping done step
# info [2026-10-26 16:31:46.757 UTC]: Step 2/2 cleaned
# info [2026-10-26 16:31:46.759 UTC]: Finished in 0.002 s (1 done, 1 skipped, 0 failed)
p[["cleaned", "out"]]
# [1] 0.33 0.67 1.00 1.33

Limits.

  • You list the helpers yourself. {targets} finds the functions a target calls, and the functions those call, by static code analysis. Here, a helper of a helper is only covered if you add it to the hash, e.g. rlang::hash(lapply(list(clean, other), utils::removeSource)).
  • Like {targets}, this does not track functions from packages. A package update does not outdate anything.

A metadata table like tar_meta()

tar_meta() returns a table with one row per target: when it ran, how long it took, the size of its output and the error if it failed.

The step table of a pipeline (pip_data()) has most of this. time_start is the start of the step’s last run. time is the end of its last successful run, so a failed step keeps the time of an earlier success (or NA). The duration is time - time_start, but only for steps that did not fail. The output of a failed step is the condition that it signalled.

meta <- function(p) {
    d <- as.data.frame(pip_data(p))
    ok <- d$state != "failed"
    seconds <- as.numeric(difftime(d$time, d$time_start, units = "secs"))
    bytes <- vapply(d$out, \(x) as.numeric(object.size(x)), numeric(1))
    error <- vapply(
        d$out,
        \(x) if (inherits(x, "error")) conditionMessage(x) else NA_character_,
        character(1)
    )
    data.frame(
        step = d$step,
        state = d$state,
        start = d$time_start,
        seconds = ifelse(ok, round(seconds, 2), NA),
        bytes = ifelse(ok, bytes, NA),
        error = error
    )
}

Let’s use it on a pipeline with a slow first step and a step that fails for large inputs.

p <- pip_new("meta") |>
    pip_add("load", \(n = 3) {
        Sys.sleep(0.2)
        seq_len(n)
    }) |>
    pip_add("fit", \(x = ~load) {
        if (length(x) > 3) stop("too many values")
        sum(x)
    }) |>
    pip_add("report", \(x = ~fit) paste("total:", x))

pip_run(p, lgr = NULL)
meta(p)
#     step state               start seconds bytes error
# 1   load  done 2026-10-26 16:31:46     0.2    64  <NA>
# 2    fit  done 2026-10-26 16:31:47     0.0    56  <NA>
# 3 report  done 2026-10-26 16:31:47     0.0   120  <NA>

Now the input grows and fit fails. With on_error = "continue", the run goes on, and report is skipped because its input failed.

pip_set_params(p, list(n = 5))
pip_run(p, lgr = NULL, on_error = "continue")
# Warning: Run of pipeline 'meta' continued after 1 failed step:
#   'fit': too many values
# Steps not run because an input failed: 'report'
meta(p)
#     step    state               start seconds bytes           error
# 1   load     done 2026-10-26 16:31:47     0.2    80            <NA>
# 2    fit   failed 2026-10-26 16:31:47      NA    NA too many values
# 3 report outdated 2026-10-26 16:31:47     0.0   120            <NA>

The table shows the error of fit. report is outdated and still has the start time and output of the first run.

Limits.

  • Only the last run of each step is recorded. Keep a history by appending meta(p) to a table after each run.
  • Warnings are not recorded, and there is no hash of the output.

Metadata stored with each output

{targets} stores metadata such as size and format along with each target.

In {pipeflow}, the generic pip_output_value() is called on every output right after its step returns. A method for your own class can attach the metadata to the output itself. See Annotated step outputs for the details.

tracked <- function(x) structure(x, class = c("tracked", class(x)))

pip_output_value.tracked <- function(x, ctx = list(), ...) {
    attr(x, "meta") <- list(
        step = ctx[["step"]],
        time = ctx[["time"]],
        class = setdiff(class(x), "tracked"),
        bytes = as.numeric(object.size(x))
    )
    x
}
registerS3method("pip_output_value", "tracked", pip_output_value.tracked)

p <- pip_new("tracked") |>
    pip_add("cars", \(n = 5) tracked(head(mtcars, n)))

pip_run(p, lgr = NULL)
str(attr(p[["cars", "out"]], "meta"))
# List of 4
#  $ step : chr "cars"
#  $ time : POSIXct[1:1], format: "2026-10-26 16:31:47"
#  $ class: chr "data.frame"
#  $ bytes: num 2976

Limits. Each step has to mark its output with the class. Methods are meant for your own classes, not for base classes such as data.frame.

Reproducible random numbers

{targets} gives each target its own seed (see tar_seed()), so a target draws the same random numbers no matter which other targets run.

In {pipeflow}, steps draw from the global random number stream. Steps that are skipped don’t draw, so the numbers a step gets depend on which steps ran before it. Here, b gets different numbers when it reruns alone than in a full run, although the seed is the same.

p <- pip_new("rng") |>
    pip_add("a", \(n = 3) rnorm(n)) |>
    pip_add("b", \(n = 3, scale = 1) scale * rnorm(n))

set.seed(1)
pip_run(p, lgr = NULL)
b_full <- p[["b", "out"]]

pip_set_params(p, list(scale = 2))
set.seed(1)
pip_run(p, lgr = NULL)
p[["b", "out"]]
# [1] -1.2529076  0.3672866 -1.6712572
2 * b_full
# [1]  3.1905616  0.6590155 -1.6409368

The recipe: give each step a seed parameter and set it inside the step. A small helper also restores the global random number state afterwards, so running the pipeline doesn’t change the numbers that the rest of your session draws. withr::with_seed() does the same, if you have {withr} installed.

with_seed <- function(seed, code) {
    old <- get0(".Random.seed", envir = globalenv(), inherits = FALSE)
    on.exit(
        if (is.null(old)) {
            rm(".Random.seed", envir = globalenv())
        } else {
            assign(".Random.seed", old, envir = globalenv())
        }
    )
    set.seed(seed)
    code
}

Now b gets the same numbers, whether it runs alone or with a.

p <- pip_new("rng") |>
    pip_add("a", \(n = 3, seed = 1) with_seed(seed, rnorm(n))) |>
    pip_add("b", \(n = 3, scale = 1, seed = 2) {
        with_seed(seed, scale * rnorm(n))
    })

pip_run(p, lgr = NULL)
b_full <- p[["b", "out"]]

pip_set_params(p, list(scale = 2))
pip_run(p, lgr = NULL)
p[["b", "out"]]
# [1] -1.7938291  0.3696984  3.1756907
2 * b_full
# [1] -1.7938291  0.3696984  3.1756907

Limits.

  • You choose the seeds. {targets} derives them from the target names.
  • pip_set_params(p, list(seed = 42)) sets the seed of all steps with a seed parameter, so they would all draw the same numbers.
  • Steps that run code in parallel need a parallel-safe generator, as with any R code.

Results that survive an R restart

{targets} stores every target on disk, so the results survive when R is restarted.

A {pipeflow} pipeline is an R object. Save it with saveRDS() after running it, and read it back with readRDS() in a new session. The functions, parameters, outputs and states are all kept. The dependency graph lives in C++ and can’t be saved directly. It is rebuilt automatically the first time the pipeline is used. Let’s save the file pipeline from above.

p <- pip_new("files") |>
    pip_add("read", \(path, rev = NULL) read.csv(path),
        params = list(path = path)
    ) |>
    pip_add("total", \(data = ~read) sum(data$x))

refresh(p) |> pip_run(lgr = NULL)

file <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
saveRDS(p, file)
rm(p)

Here, rm() stands in for the restart. After readRDS(), the steps are still done. The fingerprint of the file was saved too, so refresh() only reruns steps if the file changed in the meantime.

p <- readRDS(file)
p
# <pipeflow> files (2 steps)
# --------------------------
#     step   params depends state               out
# 1:  read path,rev          done <data.frame[4x1]>
# 2: total     data    read  done                10
# --------------------------
# <ready> last run: 2026-10-26 16:31:47 (0.002 s)
# steps: 2 done

refresh(p) |> pip_run()
# info [2026-10-26 16:31:47.803 UTC]: Starting run of pipeflow 'files'
# info [2026-10-26 16:31:47.803 UTC]: Step 1/2 read - skipping done step
# info [2026-10-26 16:31:47.803 UTC]: Step 2/2 total - skipping done step
# info [2026-10-26 16:31:47.804 UTC]: Finished in 0.001 s (0 done, 2 skipped, 0 failed)

Step functions keep their enclosing environment. If a step function was created inside another function, that environment is saved with it, including every object in it, which can make the file large. The global environment is never saved: helpers such as refresh() or with_seed() have to be defined again in the new session.

Limits.

  • Nothing is saved automatically. If R crashes during a run, the results of that run are lost. {targets} saves each target as soon as it is built.
  • The whole pipeline is one file, written and read as a whole, and it must fit in memory.

Running in a fresh R process

tar_make() runs the pipeline in a new R process by default. The results then can’t depend on objects that happen to be lying around in your session.

With {callr}, you can run a {pipeflow} pipeline in a new R process as well. The pipeline is copied to the new process, run there and copied back.

run_fresh <- function(p, ...) {
    callr::r(
        function(p, ...) {
            library(pipeflow)
            pip_run(p, ...)
            p
        },
        args = list(p, ...)
    )
}

p <- pip_new("fresh") |>
    pip_add("data", \(n = 5) seq_len(n)) |>
    pip_add("total", \(x = ~data) sum(x))

p <- run_fresh(p, lgr = NULL)
p
# <pipeflow> fresh (2 steps)
# --------------------------
#     step params depends state       out
# 1:  data      n          done 1,2,3,4,5
# 2: total      x    data  done        15
# --------------------------
# <ready> last run: 2026-10-26 16:31:48 (0.003 s)
# steps: 2 done

What you get back is a new pipeline object, so assign it (p <-). Views and other references to the old object don’t see the results.

This is also where you find out what a step needs from your session. A step that calls a function from a package you attached with library() fails in the new process, where the package is not attached.

library(tools)

p <- pip_new("fresh") |>
    pip_add("ext", \(path = "data.csv") file_ext(path))

res <- tryCatch(run_fresh(p, lgr = NULL), error = identity)
conditionMessage(res$parent)
# [1] "step 'ext': could not find function \"file_ext\""

The same holds for objects and helper functions that a step finds in the global environment of your session. Use tools::file_ext(), or put the library() and source() calls that the steps need into the function that run_fresh() runs in the new process.

Limits.

  • {callr} is not a dependency of {pipeflow}, so you need to install it.
  • The whole pipeline, with all outputs, is copied to the new process and back on every run. For large outputs, this takes time.
  • Starting a new R process takes a moment too, which you pay on every run.

Which steps are outdated?

tar_outdated() lists the targets that the next tar_make() would run.

In {pipeflow}, the state of a step tells whether it will run: new, outdated and failed steps run, done steps are skipped. So a view of these states lists what the next run does.

p <- pip_new("outdated") |>
    pip_add("a", \(x = 1) x) |>
    pip_add("b", \(a = ~a) a + 1) |>
    pip_add("c", \(b = ~b) b + 1) |>
    pip_add("d", \(y = 1) y)

pip_run(p, lgr = NULL)
pip_set_params(p, list(y = 2))
pip_view(p, state = c("new", "outdated", "failed"))
# <pipeflow_view> outdated (1 of 4 steps)
# ---------------------------------------
#    step params depends    state out
# 1:    d      y         outdated   1
# ---------------------------------------
# <ready> last run: 2026-10-26 16:31:48 (0.003 s)
# steps: 1 outdated

The view misses a done step that reruns because a step upstream of it runs. {pipeflow} functions such as pip_set_params() or pip_reset() outdate the downstream steps, so this only happens if you set a state by hand, which outdates no other step (see ?Extract.pipeflow). Here, b and c stay done, but they run again with the new output of a.

p[["a", "state"]] <- "outdated"
pip_view(p, state = c("new", "outdated", "failed"))
# <pipeflow_view> outdated (2 of 4 steps)
# ---------------------------------------
#    step params depends    state out
# 1:    a      x         outdated   1
# 2:    d      y         outdated   1
# ---------------------------------------
# <ready> last run: 2026-10-26 16:31:48 (0.003 s)
# steps: 2 outdated
pip_run(p)
# info [2026-10-26 16:31:48.827 UTC]: Starting run of pipeflow 'outdated'
# info [2026-10-26 16:31:48.827 UTC]: Step 1/4 a
# info [2026-10-26 16:31:48.829 UTC]: Step 2/4 b
# info [2026-10-26 16:31:48.830 UTC]: Step 3/4 c
# info [2026-10-26 16:31:48.832 UTC]: Step 4/4 d
# info [2026-10-26 16:31:48.833 UTC]: Finished in 0.006 s (4 done, 0 skipped, 0 failed)

Limits.

  • Locked steps are listed but skipped. Leave them out with p[state %in% c("new", "outdated", "failed") & !locked].
  • The states only know about changes made through {pipeflow}. Call refresh() from the recipes above first, so that changed files and helpers count.

What can’t be emulated

Some features of {targets} need infrastructure that {pipeflow} doesn’t have, and a few lines of code won’t change that.

  • Distributed workers. {targets} sends targets to parallel workers, also on clusters and in the cloud, via {crew}. {pipeflow} runs the steps one after another in one R session. A step can parallelize its own work, but the pipeline does not schedule steps on workers.
  • Cloud storage. {targets} can store targets in AWS S3 or Google Cloud Storage. You can upload the file from saveRDS() yourself, but there is no storage per step.
  • Data larger than RAM. {targets} keeps each target on disk and loads only what a target needs. A {pipeflow} pipeline keeps all outputs in memory. A step can return a file path instead of the data, but then you manage the files yourself.

If you need these, use {targets}. If you mainly work in an interactive session or a Shiny app, the recipes above cover a good part of the rest.
